To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the cryptographic hardness of single-periodic neurons under noise is equivalent to the worst-case lattice problem, 2) this cryptographic hardness extends to gradient-based and SQ learning algorithms, 3) this hardness is only required under small noise, and 4) in absence of noise, we can learn such single-periodic neurons with an optimal sample-complexity of $d+ 1$ samples.
1) the hardness of learning single period neurons is necessary to establish a connection between the hardness of learning neural networks and worst-case lattice problems.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
\emph{Learning a single periodic neuron under noise is computationally hard, while learning a single periodic neurons under adversarial noise is computationally tractable.}
learning periodic neural networks with small noise is as hard as solving the worst-case lattice problem, while learning them without noise is as easy as solving the CLWE detection problem.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we demonstrate the cryptographic hardness of a family of functions that can be efficiently approximated by one-layer ReLU neural networks, under small noise.
we provide the first evidence of the cryptographic hardness of a single-layer neural network under small noise, which also implies the cryptographic hardness of CLWE detection and phase retrieval.
, in the absence or presence of noise, our work shows the cryptographic hardness of the learning problem, as well as provides a polynomial-time algorithm with the optimal sample complexity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the cryptographic hardness of a family of functions can be established by adding small noise to the labels, even when the noise is exponentially smaller than the noise required for the function to be learnable in the noiseless case.
the hardness of learning single periodic neurons is a fundamental barrier to the cryptographic security of lattice-based cryptosystems.

the hardness of learning single periodic neurons over isotropic Gaussian data is equivalent to the hardness of lattice problems, and hence the hardness result is not restricted to a specific learning algorithm.
